title: I Used the Terrarium-Mist Hours on the Intern Who Left My Numbered Nozzle

parts.text: I stepped into the glass room at 11:07 a.m. and intern Jules was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE TANK. FORTY MINUTES. NOZZLES STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was twenty-six, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered nozzles. Jules shrugged. "Interns are the mist." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover moss on my numbered nozzle. Then I asked for the mist log. At 11:15 the desk pinged why Jules's name was on my moss. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Jules's leftover moss on my numbered nozzle.

social.video_title: She left my numbered terrarium nozzle on my hours — Part 1/2
social.description: Glass room, leftover moss, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the mist. Would you have asked for the mist log?

parts.text: Jules called it hardscape until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the moss still. The nozzle went back to my numbered slot. Jules ran a slot of her own and told the next intern atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: INTERNS ARE NOT THE MIST. I keep my nozzles in a labeled tray. Jules brown-bags her hardscape. The glass room finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns are not the mist — Part 2/2
social.description: Mist log, numbered nozzle, and a second line on the board. Was hardscape ever my moss?
